paras: The Dubuque jail attack on two Black roustabouts was a beating of two Black prisoners by white fellow inmates in the jail at Dubuque, Iowa, in late summer 1882. The two men were struck with chair-rounds and table-legs until court-house officers stopped what the papers called a riot. Papers outside Iowa ran the item as an example of race prejudice in the North, describing it as 'an effort to draw the color line'.

According to a widely reprinted news brief, the two men were roustabouts accused of stealing $345 from a woman sick with ague on the steamer Mary Morton, and were jailed at Dubuque. One version of the brief gave the sum as $315, and the Savannah Morning News said only that they had been jailed 'for the crime of theft'.

The Savannah Morning News, summarizing a Dubuque dispatch, wrote that the white prisoners 'took offense' at being made to associate with Black men and that 'a lively row ensued'. The news brief named the attackers as 'several Irishmen in the jail', who 'gave them a welcome with chair-rounds and table-legs'. The two men were 'pounded unmercifully', and it took all the officials or 'all the force' about the court-house to end the fight.
No report names the injured men or describes their injuries, and no report of charges against the attackers or of the outcome of the theft case was found.

The episode survives only in out-of-state papers, all drawing on one Dubuque dispatch. A short brief ran in news-summary columns, appearing in The Times of Owosso, Michigan, on September 15, in the Milan Exchange of Tennessee and the Huntsville Gazette on September 16, in the Batesville Guard of Arkansas on September 20, and in the Bolivar Bulletin and the Iron County Register on September 21. The brief treated the beating lightly, calling it a 'welcome', and stated the theft as fact; the Owosso paper headed it 'the latest outbreak of race prejudice'.

The Savannah Morning News took a partisan line, observing that Iowa was 'a strong Republican State' where one might expect 'the color line would be obliterated', yet the dispatch showed 'intense prejudice' against Black people. It quoted the Hartford Times, which asked in mock earnest whether 'the colored men' had 'no rights which white men are bound to respect' and proposed to 'resurrect the civil rights bill' for prisoners. No Iowa paper's account of the attack was found in the coverage.

accounts.label: Syndicated news brief
accounts.gist: Two Black roustabouts jailed for stealing from a sick woman on the steamer Mary Morton were given 'a welcome' with chair-rounds and table-legs by several Irishmen in the jail, and all the court-house force was needed to quell the riot.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News editorial (after a Dubuque dispatch)
accounts.gist: White prisoners took offense at being made to associate with two Black men jailed for theft, pounded them unmercifully with broken chairs and table legs, and court-house officials were called to quell the riot.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News used the episode to needle Republican Iowa, saying it showed 'intense prejudice' against Black people there, and quoted the Hartford Times's ironic remark about the 'chivalrous feelings of the white convicts'.

News-brief columns ran a jocular item ('gave them a welcome with chair-rounds and table-legs') under 'an effort to draw the color line' or 'the latest outbreak of race prejudice', stating the theft as fact.
